sections.title: A tree worth dying for
sections.intro_md:
Most people meet Rajasthan as a postcard: pink palaces, golden forts, camels on dunes. The real story of this state is how people made a rich, dense, loud culture in one of the driest places on Earth, and what they were willing to give up to keep it.

Start with a tree. The khejri is a scraggly, thorny thing whose pods are dinner and whose leaves feed goats and camels. In 1730 a village of Bishnois decided it was worth more than their lives. Nearly three centuries later, in 2026, villagers were walking 700 km across the desert to protect the same kind of trees from solar parks.

spotlights.name: The Khejarli tree-huggers
spotlights.spot_it: A white memorial and temple in a grove of thorny khejri trees outside Jodhpur, with the number 363 carved on it.
spotlights.story_md: In September 1730 soldiers of Maharaja Abhai Singh of Marwar arrived at a Bishnoi village near Jodhpur to cut khejri trees. The wood was wanted to burn lime for a new palace. A woman named Amrita Devi wrapped her arms around a tree and said she would rather die than let it fall. The axemen cut her down, then her three daughters. Villagers from across the area came and did the same thing, one after another. By the time the king called it off, **363 Bishnois** were dead. He apologised and banned tree felling in Bishnoi villages, a ban the community still enforces.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two and a half centuries before Chipko, Rajasthan had the first recorded tree-hugging protest, and it was paid for in lives.
spotlights.memory_hook: 363 people died so a desert tree could stand.

sections.title: The state in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is the **largest state in India**: 3,42,239 square km, about 10.4% of the country, nearly the size of Germany. Census 2011 counted **6.85 crore** people, seventh among states, at about 200 per square km, three-quarters of them in villages. It borders Pakistan for about 1,070 km on the west, and Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat on the other sides.

The Aravalli range splits it diagonally. North-west of the ridge is the Thar, with Jaisalmer, Barmer, Bikaner and Jodhpur. South-east are greener hills and plains, Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bharatpur. The capital is Jaipur. After a reorganisation in December 2024 the state has **41 districts** in 7 divisions. Hindi is the official language, but most people speak a Rajasthani language at home.

sections.title: Desert, ridge and salt
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan's geography is a single diagonal line. The Aravalli range runs from south-west to north-east, and it decides almost everything: rainfall, crops, where cities grew, which kingdoms were rich. West of it lies the Thar, where rain can be under 150 mm a year and a decade can hold several droughts. East of it the land is greener, with rivers like the Chambal and Banas, forests and tigers.

Water shaped the culture. People built stepwells, tanks called talab and johad, and rooftop cisterns called tanka. In 1958 India started the Indira Gandhi Canal, which now carries Punjab's river water hundreds of km into the desert along the line of an ancient dry river, turning parts of Ganganagar and Hanumangarh into wheat country.

spotlights.name: The Thar Desert

where.label: Sam dunes, 42 km west of Jaisalmer

spotlights.spot_it: Rippled orange sand dunes under a hard blue sky, with camels, thorn scrub and a village or two never far away.
spotlights.story_md: The Thar covers about **2.64 lakh square km**, most of it in western Rajasthan, and it is the eastern tip of the belt of dry land that starts in the Sahara. It is also the most crowded desert on Earth, at about 83 people per square km, because it is not empty sand: it is scrub, dunes, salt flats and villages built around ponds. Rain is 100 to 300 mm a year, most of it in July to September. Summer days pass 50°C. In 2023 scientists described a dinosaur from its rocks, *Tharosaurus indicus*, among the oldest known diplodocoid sauropods.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two-thirds of the state is shaped by this desert, from the food to the architecture to the songs.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's most crowded desert sits on a dinosaur.

spotlights.name: The Aravalli range and Guru Shikhar
spotlights.when: Among the oldest fold mountains on Earth
spotlights.spot_it: A low, worn, rocky ridge of grey and green that runs diagonally across the state; at its south end, the granite summit of Guru Shikhar with a small temple on top.
spotlights.story_md: The Aravallis run about 670 km from Gujarat through Rajasthan to the edge of Delhi, cutting the state into a dry north-west and a greener south-east. They are worn stumps of mountains that were folded up well over a billion years ago, which is why they are so low and rounded. The highest point is **Guru Shikhar, 1,722 m**, near Mount Abu. The ridge holds back sand from the east, feeds groundwater, and is the last green wall between the Thar and the Gangetic plain. In 2025 a fight over how to define it reached the Supreme Court.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The range decides where the desert stops, and it is under pressure from mining.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old enough to be nearly worn flat, still the only wall the desert has.

spotlights.name: Sambhar Salt Lake
spotlights.spot_it: A flat white plain to the horizon, crusted with salt, with pink flamingos in a thin film of water after the rains.
spotlights.story_md: India's largest inland salt lake spreads over **190 to 230 square km**, depending on the season, about 80 km west of Jaipur. Its water is three to four times saltier than the sea. In good years tens of thousands of greater and lesser flamingos winter here. In November 2019 the lake turned into a graveyard: somewhere between 15,000 and 23,000 migratory birds died of avian botulism, one of the worst bird die-offs India has recorded. In legend, the goddess Shakambhari turned a forest of jewels into salt so that people would stop fighting over it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a salt factory, a bird refuge and an early warning of what heat and pollution do to wetlands.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess turned treasure into salt so nobody would fight over it.

spotlights.name: Great Indian bustard (godawan)
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, long-necked bird pacing on grassland, white neck, black cap, sandy-brown back, about a metre high.
spotlights.story_md: The godawan is one of the heaviest flying birds in the world: males weigh 8 to 14.5 kg and stand about a metre tall. In 1969 there were about **1,260**; by 2018, fewer than **150**, most of them around Jaisalmer. The biggest killer is the power line: a heavy bird with eyes on the sides of its head cannot see the wires in time. Since 2019 a breeding centre at Sam and another at Ramdevra have raised birds from wild eggs. In 2024 a chick hatched from artificial insemination, with sperm carried from a male 200 km away, and eight more chicks hatched in March and April 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a test of whether India's solar boom and its rarest bird can share the same land.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bird the size of a child, killed by a wire it cannot see.

spotlights.name: Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur
spotlights.spot_it: Shallow marsh, acacia islands and painted storks nesting so thickly that the trees look white.
spotlights.story_md: Keoladeo is only about **29 square km**, yet more than 370 bird species have been recorded in it. It is not a natural marsh. The Maharajas of Bharatpur flooded a natural depression with canal water in the late 1800s to make a private duck shoot, and invited viceroys to compete. A stone tablet in the park lists their bags; the largest is credited to the viceroy Lord Linlithgow in 1938, at more than 4,000 birds in a day. The last Siberian cranes, a western flock that wintered here, were seen in 2001-02 and have not come back.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A royal killing ground became one of Asia's great bird refuges.
spotlights.memory_hook: The best bird park in India was built so kings could shoot ducks.

spotlights.name: Ranthambore's tigers
spotlights.spot_it: A tiger walking past the ruins of a thousand-year-old fort and lakeside pavilions in dry forest.
spotlights.story_md: Ranthambore is the rare tiger reserve where tigers walk through medieval ruins: the fort on its hill dates back about a thousand years and is a UNESCO site. Its most famous resident was a tigress called **Machli**, often called the most photographed tiger in the world, who killed a mugger crocodile in a fight at a lake in 2003, losing two canine teeth, and died in 2016 at 19, very old for a wild tiger. In 2008 two of her daughters were among the tigers moved to Sariska, a reserve near Alwar where poachers had killed every tiger by 2004-05. Sariska now has tigers again. Rajasthan also holds Mukundra Hills and Ramgarh Vishdhari reserves.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a desert state can hold tigers, and that a reserve can lose them all.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tigress who fought a crocodile and became the most photographed cat alive.

spotlights.name: The camel and the Raika herders
spotlights.spot_it: A one-humped dromedary with tassels and a painted saddle, led by a man in a big red turban.
spotlights.story_md: Rajasthan holds most of India's camels and made the camel a state animal in 2014. The next year it passed a law banning camel slaughter and the movement of camels out of the state. The intent was protection. The effect, herders say, was to wreck the market: a camel you cannot sell is a cost. India's camel count fell from about **4 lakh in 2012 to about 2.5 lakh in 2019**, and most of the fall was in Rajasthan. The Raika, or Rebari, are the camel's traditional keepers, a pastoral people who walk herds hundreds of km through the year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The camel built the desert's trade routes; its decline is a measure of how fast the desert is changing.
spotlights.memory_hook: A law to save the camel made it worthless to own one.

sections.title: Five thousand years of the desert's past
sections.intro_md:
People farmed here before almost anywhere else in South Asia. Kalibangan, on the dry Ghaggar river, was an Indus town by about 2900 BCE. Later the Matsya kingdom had its capital at Bairat near Jaipur, and the Mauryan emperor Ashoka left an inscription there.

The Rajputs, the warrior clans that gave the region its old name, Rajputana, rose from about the 7th century. The Gurjara-Pratiharas held back Arab armies in the 8th century. Prithviraj Chauhan of Ajmer beat Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain in 1191 and lost to him there in 1192, opening north India to the Delhi Sultanate. From then on the region's story is often told as sieges: Ranthambore in 1301, Chittor in 1303, 1535 and 1568.

The truth is more complicated. Most Rajput kingdoms allied with the Mughals, served in their armies and married into their family, while Mewar resisted. In 1818 most states signed treaties with the British.

spotlights.name: Kalibangan

where.label: Hanumangarh district, on the dry Ghaggar

spotlights.spot_it: Low mud-brick mounds and excavated walls on a flat plain beside a dry riverbed in the far north of the state.
spotlights.story_md: Kalibangan means black bangles in the local Bagri dialect, after the shards of terracotta bangles scattered on the mounds. An Italian scholar, Luigi Pio Tessitori, spotted the ruins as prehistoric around 1917. Excavated from 1960 to 1969, they turned out to be an Indus city on the banks of the Ghaggar, now dry. Two finds are world-class. One is a **ploughed field from about 2800 BCE**, criss-crossed with furrows, among the oldest ever found. The other is evidence of an earthquake around 2600 BCE that seems to have ended the early town, possibly the oldest earthquake known from archaeology.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rajasthan's story starts as one of the world's first cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black bangles, a 4,800-year-old field, and the oldest dug-up earthquake.

spotlights.name: Chittorgarh Fort
spotlights.spot_it: A fortified plateau 180 m above the plain with a 13 km wall, palaces, water tanks and a nine-storey tower.
spotlights.story_md: Chittor is one of the largest forts in India, about 280 hectares on a long hill, with a perimeter of 13 km. It was Mewar's capital, and it fell three times. In **1303** Alauddin Khalji took it after an eight-month siege. In **1535** Bahadur Shah of Gujarat sacked it, and Rani Karnavati is said to have led the women into the fire of jauhar while the men rode out to die. In **1568** Akbar besieged it for about four months and massacred tens of thousands after it fell. The Padmini story comes from a poem of 1540 and is treated as legend.
spotlights.why_it_matters: In Rajasthan's memory, Chittor stands for choosing death over surrender.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three sieges, three fires, one hill.

spotlights.name: Vijay Stambh, Tower of Victory
spotlights.spot_it: A slim nine-storey tower of carved sandstone with windows on every level and a small dome on top.
spotlights.story_md: Rana Kumbha built this 37 m tower to celebrate his victory over Mahmud Khalji, Sultan of Malwa, in 1440. You can climb its **157 steps** through nine storeys, and every surface inside and out is carved with Hindu gods, so it works as a sculpture museum stacked vertically. The names of the builders, the architect Jaita and his sons, are inscribed on it, which is rare. A few hundred metres away stands the older and smaller Kirti Stambh, the Tower of Fame, built by a Jain merchant in the 12th century for the first Tirthankara, Adinath.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the emblem of Rajasthan Police and a model for how Rajput kings advertised their power.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine storeys of gods, built to say: I won.

compare.difference: The Kirti Stambh is older (12th century), shorter at 22 m and Jain; the Vijay Stambh is Hindu, royal and 15th century.

spotlights.name: Kumbhalgarh, the 36 km wall
spotlights.spot_it: A thick crenellated wall snaking over the Aravalli ridges for as far as you can see, round towers every few hundred metres.
spotlights.story_md: Rana Kumbha's architect Mandan began this fort in the 1440s, about 1,100 m up in the Aravallis. Its wall runs about **36 km**, wide enough in places for several horses to ride side by side, and it is often called the Great Wall of India. Inside are more than 360 temples, most of them Jain. Maharana Pratap was born here in 1540. The fort fell once, to the Mughal general Shahbaz Khan in 1578 after a long siege, and Pratap took it back in 1583.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was Mewar's refuge when Chittor was lost.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wall so long it needs its own name: the Great Wall of India.

spotlights.name: Maharana Pratap and Haldighati
spotlights.spot_it: A moustached warrior on a rearing horse, spear raised, a war elephant ahead; or a narrow pass with yellow earth.
spotlights.story_md: Pratap ruled Mewar from 1572 to 1597 and never accepted Akbar as overlord when most Rajput houses had. On **18 June 1576** his army met a Mughal force led by Man Singh of Amber, a Rajput, at the Haldighati pass, named for its turmeric-yellow soil. Pratap's vanguard was led by an Afghan, Hakim Khan Sur. The Mughals won the field, Pratap escaped wounded, and he spent two decades in guerrilla war, retaking most of Mewar but not Chittor. The famous image of his horse Chetak leaping onto an elephant is legend. In 2017 there was a push to rewrite school textbooks to say Pratap won; historians disagreed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is Rajasthan's model of defiance, and a lesson in how history gets turned into politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rajputs on both sides, an Afghan in Pratap's front line, and a yellow pass.

sections.title: From Rajputana to Rajasthan
sections.intro_md:
The 18th century gave Rajasthan its best known city. In 1727 Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber moved his capital to a planned city on the plain and named it after himself.

In the 19th century the British ran the states through the Rajputana Agency and left the princes alone as long as they stayed loyal. In 1947 most signed up to India quickly, and over eight years Sardar Patel's ministry merged the pieces into one state.

After independence the desert gained a new and very different role. Its emptiness and its border made it the place where India tested its nuclear weapons, at Pokhran in 1974 and 1998.

spotlights.name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
spotlights.spot_it: Giant geometric stone shapes in a courtyard: a staircase-like triangle 27 m tall, bowls, arcs and rings.
spotlights.story_md: Sawai Jai Singh II, the king who founded Jaipur, was an astronomer who did not trust brass instruments because they were too small to be accurate. So he built them in stone, at room size. Jaipur's observatory has **19 instruments**. The biggest, the Samrat Yantra, is a sundial 27 m tall whose shadow moves about 1 mm a second, and it tells local time to about **two seconds**. He built four more observatories, in Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. Jaipur's is the largest and best preserved, and became a UNESCO site in 2010.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest stone observatory ever built, and still works.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sundial so big you can watch the shadow crawl.

spotlights.name: The Pink City
spotlights.spot_it: Long straight bazaars with terracotta-pink arcades, white trim and identical shopfronts.
spotlights.story_md: Jaipur was founded on **18 November 1727** by Sawai Jai Singh II and laid out by a Bengali engineer-scholar, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, on a grid of nine blocks drawn from Vastu Shastra, with streets 34 m wide. That made it one of the first planned cities of its age in India. The colour came later: in 1876 Maharaja Ram Singh II had the old city painted pink, the colour of welcome, for a visit by the Prince of Wales. It stayed. In 2019 the walled city was inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage City. The Jaipur foot, a cheap artificial leg used around the world, was invented here in 1968.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the model of a planned Indian city, two centuries before Chandigarh.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole city painted for one royal guest, and kept that way.

spotlights.name: Twenty-two states become one
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of maharajas in turbans and achkans signing papers with Indian officials.
spotlights.story_md: In 1947 there was no Rajasthan. There was Rajputana: **19 princely states, 3 chiefships and British Ajmer-Merwara**. The name Rajasthan had been popularised by a British officer, James Tod, whose *Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan* (1829 to 1832) romanticised Rajput history. Merging them took seven stages, from the Matsya Union of March 1948 to the final addition of Ajmer, Abu and Sunel Tappa on **1 November 1956**. The key day was **30 March 1949**, when Jaipur, Jodhpur, Bikaner and Jaisalmer joined, still celebrated as Rajasthan Day. Sawai Man Singh II of Jaipur became the first Rajpramukh, a sort of governor for life. Princes kept privy purses until Indira Gandhi abolished them in 1971.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why Rajasthan has so many old capitals and so many royal families still in politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rajasthan was born in seven instalments.

spotlights.name: Pokhran, the nuclear desert
spotlights.spot_it: A flat, scrubby test range in the Thar; in photos, a shallow crater and a group of men in army fatigues.
spotlights.story_md: India's first nuclear test, code-named Smiling Buddha, was set off under the Thar at Pokhran on **18 May 1974**, which was Buddha Purnima. The second series, Operation Shakti, came on **11 and 13 May 1998**: five devices. To hide the preparations from American satellites, scientists worked at night, wore army uniforms and moved equipment when the satellites were not overhead. The world found out when the government announced it. 11 May is now National Technology Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where India became a declared nuclear power.
spotlights.memory_hook: Scientists in army fatigues, hiding from satellites in the sand.

sections.title: Forts, palaces and a stepwell
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is famous for its forts and palaces, and you can read its history in their shapes. Hill forts like Chittor and Kumbhalgarh were built to hold out for months. Palaces like Amber and the City Palace in Udaipur show what alliance with the Mughals paid for: courtyards, mirror halls, painted ceilings. Six hill forts, Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer, were listed together by UNESCO in 2013.

Many are still owned by former royal families, who after 1971 lost their privy purses and turned palaces into hotels and museums. That decision, born from loss, made heritage tourism the state's signature industry.

Not all great buildings here are for kings. The stepwell, a stone staircase down to the water table, was built by rulers, merchants and pious widows, and served everyone.

spotlights.name: Amber Fort
spotlights.when: Begun 1592 by Raja Man Singh I
spotlights.spot_it: Honey-coloured walls climbing a ridge above a lake; inside, a hall with ceilings and walls of tiny mirrors.
spotlights.story_md: Amber was the capital of the Kachhwaha Rajputs before Jaipur. The present palace was begun in 1592 by Raja Man Singh I, the same Man Singh who led Akbar's army at Haldighati: the Kachhwahas were Akbar's closest Rajput allies, and a Kachhwaha princess married him in 1562. That alliance paid for the palace. Its most famous room, the Sheesh Mahal, is covered in convex mirror pieces so that a single candle fills the room with stars. The fort is linked by a wall to Jaigarh above it, which holds what is often called the largest cannon on wheels, Jaivana. Amber became a UNESCO site in 2013.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest picture of how Rajput and Mughal power fused.
spotlights.memory_hook: One candle, a thousand mirrors, a night sky indoors.

spotlights.name: Mehrangarh, Jodhpur
spotlights.spot_it: A fort that seems to grow out of a 120 m cliff, walls up to 36 m high, above a city of blue houses.
spotlights.story_md: Rao Jodha of the Rathores laid the foundation on **12 May 1459**. Its walls rise up to 36 m and are about 21 m thick. The story goes that a hermit living on the hill was evicted and cursed the fort with drought, and that a man named Raja Ram Meghwal agreed to be buried alive in the foundations to make the site lucky; his descendants were given land and still live on it. Kipling called it a work of Titans. In 2008 a stampede at the temple inside killed 224 people. The fort is still owned by the former royal family and runs one of India's best museums.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best preserved and best run of the great Rajput forts.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built on a curse and a man buried alive.

spotlights.name: Jaisalmer, the living fort
spotlights.spot_it: A golden sandstone fort with 99 round bastions on a hill in the desert, houses and hotels packed inside its walls.
spotlights.story_md: Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati Rajputs founded it in **1156**, and it grew rich on caravans carrying spices, silk and opium between India and Central Asia. It is one of the few forts in the world that people still live in: about **4,000 residents**, with shops, temples and guesthouses inside the 99 bastions. That life is also its danger. Pipes and drains added for hotels push water into the soft sandstone, and parts of the walls and a queen's palace have collapsed. In 1974 Satyajit Ray filmed *Sonar Kella*, The Golden Fortress, here, and Bengali tourists have come ever since.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a test of whether a monument can stay alive without being loved to death.
spotlights.memory_hook: A golden fort slowly melting from its own bathwater.

spotlights.name: Hawa Mahal, Palace of Winds
spotlights.spot_it: A five-storey pink sandstone honeycomb of 953 small latticed windows on a busy street, almost no depth behind it.
spotlights.story_md: Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh had Lal Chand Ustad build it in **1799** so that the women of the court, who lived in purdah, could watch processions on the street without being seen. The facade has **953 small windows**, or jharokhas, with stone lattice that also pulls a breeze through. The shape is said to imitate Krishna's crown. What everybody photographs is the back: the entrance is on the other side, from the palace. It is about one room deep at the top and has ramps rather than stairs to the upper floors. It is less a palace than a screen, a building made for watching.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the logo of Jaipur and a monument to a life lived behind screens.
spotlights.memory_hook: 953 windows, and the famous side is the back.

spotlights.name: Lake Palace, Udaipur
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble palace that seems to float on a lake, with the long City Palace on the shore behind it.
spotlights.story_md: Maharana Jagat Singh II built Jag Niwas on a 1.6 hectare island in Lake Pichola as a summer palace. Udaipur itself was founded in 1559 by Udai Singh II after Chittor became too exposed, and its lakes are artificial, dammed in the 14th to 17th centuries. In 1963 the palace became a hotel, and the Taj group has run it since 1971. It played the home of the villain Octopussy in the 1983 James Bond film, and Udaipur still shows *Octopussy* on a loop in a few rooftop restaurants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Udaipur is the reason Rajasthan is sold as romance.
spotlights.memory_hook: James Bond's villain lived on a lake that people dug by hand.

spotlights.name: Chand Baori stepwell
spotlights.spot_it: An inverted pyramid of zigzag stairs on three sides, dropping 13 levels to a square green pool.
spotlights.story_md: In a land where rain comes for three months, the rich built stepwells so people could reach the water table all year. Chand Baori in Abhaneri is about **30 m deep**, with about **3,500 narrow steps** arranged in a criss-cross pattern down 13 levels. The air at the bottom is said to be 5 to 6°C cooler than at the top, so it was also a place to sit out the summer. It dates from about the 8th or 9th century. It has appeared in films including *Paheli* and *The Fall*, and inspired the prison pit in *The Dark Knight Rises*.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Stepwells are the desert's engineering: water, shade and social life in one hole.
spotlights.memory_hook: 3,500 steps down to a pool, with nowhere to hide.

sections.title: How Rajasthan talks
sections.intro_md:
Officially, Rajasthan speaks Hindi. At home, most people speak one of the Rajasthani languages: Marwari around Jodhpur and Bikaner, Mewari around Udaipur, Dhundhari around Jaipur, Hadauti around Kota, Wagdi among Bhils in the south, Shekhawati in the north-east. In the 2011 census about **37% reported Rajasthani** as their mother tongue and 27% Hindi, with Marwari, Mewari, Wagdi and Hadauti counted separately.

The language has a long literature. It is named Maru Bhasa, the desert tongue, in a text from 778 CE. Charan bards wrote heroic poetry in a high literary style called Dingal, full of battle and praise.

What Rajasthani does not have is a place in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. The state assembly asked for it unanimously in 2003, and the demand is still pending. A common greeting is *Khamma ghani*, and the famous welcome song is *Padharo mhare des*: come to my land.

sections.title: Gods, saints and rats
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is a Hindu-majority state with a deep Jain and Sufi layer, and a folk religion that matters as much as the big temples. Village gods like Pabuji, Ramdev and Tejaji were often local heroes who died protecting cattle or the weak.

Jain merchants paid for some of the finest temples in India, at Mount Abu and Ranakpur. Ajmer has the most visited Sufi shrine in South Asia. Pushkar is one of the holiest towns of Hinduism. And Bikaner has a temple where rats are holy. Bhakti came through Mirabai, whose songs are sung far beyond the state.

spotlights.name: Dilwara temples, Mount Abu
spotlights.spot_it: Plain from outside; inside, white marble carved so finely that ceilings look like lace or frozen foam.
spotlights.story_md: Five Jain temples sit in a walled compound in the hills. The oldest, Vimal Vasahi, was built around **1031** by Vimal Shah, a minister of the Chaulukya king of Gujarat. The second, Luna Vasahi, was built in **1230** by two minister brothers, Vastupal and Tejpal. The marble had to be hauled up the mountain. A story says the carvers were paid in gold according to the weight of the marble dust they scraped off, which was a way of rewarding fine work. The domed ceilings are the high point: concentric rings of dancers, musicians and lotus petals that end in a hanging pendant at the centre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Many think these are the finest marble carvings in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Carvers paid in gold by the weight of the dust.

spotlights.name: Ranakpur Jain temple
spotlights.spot_it: A forest of carved pale marble pillars in shafts of light, every one different.
spotlights.story_md: A Jain merchant, Dharna Shah, began this temple to the first Tirthankara, Adinath, around 1437, on land given by Rana Kumbha, with an architect named Depaka. It stands on **1,444 marble pillars**, and the tradition is that no two are carved alike. The plan is four-faced, so you can approach the main shrine from all four sides, and light falls into the halls from many small domes. One pillar is said to be left unfinished on purpose. An image of Parshvanatha is carved from a single slab with 1,008 snake heads. Legend says you can never count the pillars the same way twice.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the wealth of Rajasthan's Jain merchants, who also funded much of its trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1,444 pillars, and none of them repeat.

spotlights.name: Karni Mata, the rat temple
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of brown rats drinking from steel bowls of milk on a marble floor, beside silver doors.
spotlights.story_md: About **20,000 rats**, called kaba, live in this temple at Deshnoke. The story is that Karni Mata, a 14th to 15th century holy woman of the Charan community, asked the god of death to return a drowned boy; when refused, she vowed that her people would be reborn as rats in her temple, and the rats as Charans. So the rats are kin. They eat from the same bowls as the priests, food they have nibbled is a blessing, and if you kill one by accident the custom is to replace it with one of gold or silver. The silver doors were given by Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most extreme example of how Rajasthan's folk faith treats animals as family.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kill a rat here and you owe the temple a gold one.

spotlights.name: Ajmer Sharif Dargah
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble shrine with a silver-plated dome, packed with pilgrims carrying baskets of red roses and green chadars.
spotlights.story_md: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, a Sufi from Persia, settled in Ajmer in the late 12th century and died there in **1236**. His tomb became the most visited Sufi shrine in South Asia, for Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs alike. Akbar walked here from Agra on foot after the birth of his son Salim, and the shrine's two giant cauldrons, or degs, are associated with Akbar and Jahangir. During the six-day Urs, the anniversary of the saint's death, the cauldrons are used to cook a sweet rice dish for the crowds.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a Rajasthan whose faith is older and more mixed than its battle stories.
spotlights.memory_hook: An emperor walked here barefoot for a son.

spotlights.name: Pushkar and its Brahma temple
spotlights.spot_it: A small lake ringed by white ghats and temples, with a red spire on the Brahma temple and hills on three sides.
spotlights.story_md: Pushkar is one of the holiest towns in India, built around a lake said to have formed where a lotus fell from Brahma's hand. Its temple is one of the very few in the world dedicated to Brahma. The usual explanation is a legend: Brahma held a ritual without his wife Savitri, married a stand-in, and Savitri cursed him to be worshipped almost nowhere. She has her own temple on a hill above the town. The lake has 52 ghats; some of Mahatma Gandhi's ashes were immersed at one of them in 1948, now called Gandhi Ghat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where faith, tourism and a giant livestock fair meet.
spotlights.memory_hook: The creator of the universe, cursed to have almost no temples.

spotlights.name: Mirabai
spotlights.spot_it: In paintings: a woman in white with a tanpura, singing before an image of Krishna.
spotlights.story_md: Mira was a Rajput princess from Merta who married into the royal house of Mewar, to a son of Rana Sanga. She refused to behave like a royal widow: she sang and danced in public, mixed with holy men of all castes, and said her real husband was Krishna. Her in-laws, the legends say, sent her a cup of poison and a snake in a basket, and she survived both. Hundreds of songs are credited to her, though scholars think many were written later in her name. She is said to have died in Dwarka, Krishna's city in Gujarat. Her songs, like *Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo*, are still sung across India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is India's best known woman poet-saint and a rebel against Rajput court rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen who said her husband was a god.

sections.title: Dance, music, puppets
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan's performing arts were built on patronage. Hereditary castes of musicians, bards and genealogists served particular families for generations: the Manganiyars and Langas sang for Rajputs and others, Charans and Bhats kept praise poetry and family histories, Bhopas sang the epics of folk gods. When the princely states vanished and villages modernised, many of these artists lost their patrons and found new ones in tourists, festivals and the world-music circuit.

The instruments are as distinctive as the songs: the kamaicha and the sarangi, the ravanhattha spike fiddle, the khartal clappers, the morchang mouth harp and the been gourd pipe. Chari dancers balance lit pots on their heads; Bhavai dancers balance a stack of brass pots while standing on a sword.

spotlights.name: Ghoomar

where.label: Across Rajasthan, especially Jodhpur and Jaipur

spotlights.spot_it: Women in long, heavily pleated skirts turning slowly in a circle, faces half veiled, the skirts flaring into wheels.
spotlights.story_md: Ghoomar comes from the word for spinning. It began with the Bhil tribe and was adopted by the Rajput courts, where women of the household danced it at weddings and festivals. The skirt, the ghaghra, can carry dozens of flared panels, so a slow turn becomes a wide coloured wheel. Movements are graceful and restrained: clapping, small steps, hands rising and falling. The 2018 film *Padmaavat* turned its Ghoomar song into a national hit and a national argument, when the filmmakers digitally covered the actor's midriff after protests.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the signature dance of Rajasthani women.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spinning skirt that becomes a wheel of colour.

spotlights.name: Kalbelia

where.label: Pali, Ajmer, Chittorgarh and Udaipur districts

spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a black skirt embroidered with mirrors and silver thread whirling and bending like a snake, to the drone of a gourd pipe.
spotlights.story_md: The Kalbelia were snake catchers, travelling with cobras in baskets while the men played the been, a pipe made from a gourd, and the women danced. When India's Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 made keeping snakes illegal, the community lost its trade and the dance became the trade. The moves imitate snakes: twisting, back bends, fast spins. In 2010 UNESCO listed Kalbelia songs and dances as intangible heritage. Its star, **Gulabo Sapera**, has said that as a newborn girl she was buried alive and rescued by her mother and aunt; she went on to dance for audiences worldwide and received the Padma Shri in 2016.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A community that lost its living to wildlife law turned its dance into a global stage act.
spotlights.memory_hook: Snake charmers without snakes, dancing like the snakes.

spotlights.name: Manganiyar musicians and the kamaicha
spotlights.spot_it: Men in bright turbans singing full-throated, one bowing a round-bellied fiddle, another clacking wooden blocks in each hand.
spotlights.story_md: The Manganiyars are Muslim hereditary musicians whose patrons, the jajmans, are mostly Hindu Rajput families. They sing at their patrons' births and weddings, and in return were paid in grain, cash or camels. They carry genealogies and battle stories in their songs, so they are called the oral historians of the desert. Their signature instrument is the **kamaicha**, a bowed fiddle with a mango-wood body covered in goat skin and up to 17 strings. Sakar Khan, a kamaicha master, received the Padma Shri. In Roysten Abel's stage show *The Manganiyar Seduction*, dozens of singers sit in lit boxes stacked like a puppet theatre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Their music is the soundtrack of Rajasthan, and a living case of Hindu-Muslim patronage.
spotlights.memory_hook: Muslim singers keeping Hindu family trees.

spotlights.name: Pabuji ki phad
spotlights.spot_it: A long cloth crowded with flat red, yellow and green figures, a hero on a black mare at the centre, unrolled at night behind a singer with a fiddle.
spotlights.story_md: A phad is a portable temple. Bhopas, priest-singers, carry these painted scrolls from village to village and unroll them after dark. The Bhopa sings the epic of Pabuji, a 14th century Rathore hero who brought camels to Rajasthan and died defending a woman's cattle, while playing the ravanhattha, a spike fiddle. His wife, the Bhopi, holds up a lamp to light each scene as he points at it. The full epic is about 4,000 lines and can take five nights. The scrolls are painted by the Joshi family of Shahpura. A worn-out phad is retired by immersing it in Pushkar lake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is cinema before cinema: a screen, a light and a story told over nights.
spotlights.memory_hook: A scroll that becomes a temple when the lamp is lit.

spotlights.name: Kathputli string puppets
spotlights.spot_it: Wooden puppets with big painted eyes, turbans and long flared skirts, hanging from strings, often with no legs.
spotlights.story_md: Kathputli means wooden doll. The puppeteers, from the Bhat community, carve heads from mango wood and dress the bodies in scraps of bright cloth. Most Rajasthani puppets have no legs; the long skirt hides that. The puppeteer speaks through a reed in his mouth, the boli, which gives the shrill squeaking voice, while a woman of the family sings and drums. The stories are about heroes like Amar Singh Rathore, a 17th century noble who defied the Mughal court. Many Bhat families moved to Delhi's Kathputli Colony, a home for street performers for about half a century, which was cleared for redevelopment in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of India's oldest forms of puppetry and a craft in danger.
spotlights.memory_hook: Puppets with no legs and a voice that squeaks through a reed.

sections.title: Cloth, colour and clay
sections.intro_md:
Few places produce as many crafts as Rajasthan, and almost all of them deal with one problem: how to make a beige land bright. Women's skirts and odhnis are tie-dyed, block printed or embroidered with mirrors and gota, a gold or silver ribbon.

Craft is still organised by village and community. The Chhipas print in Bagru and Sanganer, the Joshis paint phads in Shahpura, the Kumhars of Molela make clay plaques of gods, weavers in Kaithoon make Kota Doria. Jaipur is also India's capital of gem cutting, especially emeralds, and of enamel jewellery called meenakari.

Many crafts have Geographical Indication tags. Most are threatened by power looms and screen printing that copy the look at a fraction of the price.

spotlights.name: Bandhani and leheriya
spotlights.spot_it: Cloth covered in tiny raised dots in rings and patterns (bandhani), or diagonal rainbow stripes like waves (leheriya).
spotlights.story_md: Both are tie-dye. For bandhani, women pinch the cloth into thousands of tiny points and bind each with thread before dyeing, so each dot is a resist; a fine odhni can carry tens of thousands of knots, and the dots are often still raised when you buy it. Leheriya, meaning wave, is made by rolling the cloth diagonally and binding it at intervals, then dyeing it again and again, to make zigzag stripes. Leheriya is worn in the monsoon, especially at Teej, when green and saffron waves are everywhere. Colour codes matter: red bandhani for brides, yellow and red for new mothers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rajasthani dress is coded colour; these two techniques are the vocabulary.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sari of ten thousand knots.

spotlights.name: Jaipur blue pottery
spotlights.spot_it: Glossy white bowls, tiles and vases painted in cobalt and turquoise flowers and birds.
spotlights.story_md: The surprise is that it contains no clay. The body is a frit of ground quartz, powdered glass, Multani mitti (fuller's earth), borax and gum, much like Egyptian faience. It is fired once, at low heat, which makes it fragile but means it does not craze. The technique came with Persian and Central Asian craftsmen and was nearly extinct in Jaipur by the 1950s. The painter Kripal Singh Shekhawat revived it, backed by Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Rajmata Gayatri Devi. Old blue tiles line fountains in Jaipur's Rambagh Palace. It has a GI tag.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a Persian craft that became a Jaipur signature, and a revival success.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pottery with no clay in it.

spotlights.name: Sanganer and Bagru block prints
spotlights.spot_it: Cotton printed with small repeating flowers and paisleys: delicate colours on white (Sanganer) or earthy black and red on a cream-brown ground (Bagru).
spotlights.story_md: Two villages near Jaipur, 30 km apart, have printed cloth with carved teak blocks for centuries. Sanganer prints fine motifs on white cloth, washed in the river and bleached in the sun. Bagru, the Chhipa printers' village, uses natural dyes: black from rusted iron and jaggery, red from alizarin, and a mud resist called dabu, then dries the cloth on open ground. A single bedcover can need hundreds of impressions, each lined up by eye. The fashion brand Anokhi, founded in Jaipur in 1970, made Sanganeri prints global. Both have Geographical Indication tags.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of the hand block print sold in India and abroad traces back to these two villages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black ink made of rust and jaggery.

spotlights.name: Bani Thani and Kishangarh painting
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in profile with an impossibly long, arched eye, a sharp nose and a tall forehead, holding the edge of a veil.
spotlights.story_md: Rajput painting split into many court schools: Mewar, Marwar, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh. The most famous single image is *Bani Thani*, painted at Kishangarh around 1750, usually credited to Nihal Chand. It is said to show a court singer loved by the poet-prince Sawant Singh, painted as Radha. The style exaggerates everything: lotus-petal eyes that run almost to the ear, arched brows, a long neck. It is often called India's Mona Lisa. India put it on a postage stamp in 1973. Other schools are recognisable too: Mewar paintings are flat and red-heavy; Kota paintings are full of hunting scenes in jungles.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the face that defines Rajasthani miniature painting.
spotlights.memory_hook: An eye that stretches almost to the ear.

spotlights.name: Shekhawati's painted havelis
spotlights.spot_it: Courtyard mansions whose every wall is covered in paintings of gods, elephants, steam trains, motor cars and Europeans in hats.
spotlights.story_md: Shekhawati, in the north-east of the state, is often called the world's largest open-air art gallery. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, Marwari merchants from these dusty towns made fortunes in Calcutta and Bombay and sent money home to build havelis, then competed to cover them in fresco. So you see Krishna next to a steam train, a Wright brothers aeroplane, a British gentleman with a gramophone. Many families never came back, and their havelis are now padlocked, crumbling or turned into hotels. The Birla, Goenka, Bajaj and Poddar families trace their roots to this region.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where you can read the story of Indian capitalism painted on walls.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna next to a steam train.

sections.title: Food built for drought
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthani food is the cuisine of a place where water and fresh vegetables were scarce. So it uses lots of ghee, milk, buttermilk and yoghurt instead of water; it cooks with dried beans, berries and lentil dumplings that keep for months; and it relies on millets like bajra that grow on little rain. Gatte, gram-flour dumplings in a yoghurt curry, are a vegetable dish made with no vegetables.

There are two kitchens. The Marwari and Jain merchant kitchen is vegetarian, often without onion and garlic, and rich in sweets. The Rajput kitchen is famous for game and mutton, cooked with red chillies. Both meet in festival food: dal baati churma, ghevar, and huge thalis.

spotlights.name: Dal baati churma
spotlights.spot_it: Hard, round wheat dumplings split open and drowned in ghee, next to a bowl of mixed dal and a heap of sweet crumbly churma.
spotlights.story_md: The baati is a dense ball of wheat dough that was traditionally baked in the embers of dried cow-dung cakes, or, in the version told about soldiers, buried in hot sand and left to cook. It keeps for days, which suits desert life and war. It is cracked open and soaked in ghee, eaten with panchmel dal, a dal of five lentils. Churma began, the story goes, when a cook accidentally dropped baati into sugarcane juice; today it is baati crushed with ghee and jaggery or sugar. The meal is heavy by design: made for long days with little water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the defining dish of Rajasthan, at weddings and roadside dhabas alike.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bread you bake under sand and drown in ghee.

spotlights.name: Laal maas
spotlights.spot_it: A fiery red mutton curry with a slick of oil on top, dark-red from dried chillies, eaten with bajra roti.
spotlights.story_md: Laal maas, red meat, is mutton cooked hot with **Mathania chillies**, a long red chilli grown near Jodhpur that gives colour more than burn. The story is that it began as a way to cook wild game, boar or deer, on hunts, and that the heavy spice hid the gamey smell. It sits uneasily with the image of Rajasthan as vegetarian, but the Rajput and Muslim cooks of the courts were great meat cooks. Its cousins are safed maas, white meat in a cashew and cream sauce, and jungli maas, with only chilli, salt and ghee.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the vegetarian image of Rajasthan is only half the story.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hunter's curry made red with Jodhpur chillies.

spotlights.name: Ker sangri
spotlights.spot_it: A dark, dry, tangy stir-fry of thin bean pods and small round berries, often served with bajra roti.
spotlights.story_md: Sangri are the pods of the khejri, the same tree the Bishnois died for. Ker are the pea-sized berries of a leafless desert shrub. Both are picked in spring, boiled, dried in the sun and stored for the year, which is how desert households cooked vegetables without vegetables. Cooked with dried mango, red chilli and oil, they make a sour, chewy dish that keeps for days. Today it is a delicacy, and dried sangri can sell at over a thousand rupees a kilo in cities. Its supply is falling: khejri tree density on farmland dropped from about 90 per hectare in the 1950s and 60s to about 35 in the 2010s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the purest desert food: wild, dried and stored against drought.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dinner from the tree people died to save.

spotlights.name: Bikaneri bhujia
spotlights.spot_it: Thin, crisp, pale-orange fried noodles of gram and moth bean flour, sold by the kilo in plastic packets.
spotlights.story_md: Bhujia is made from the flour of moth beans, a hardy desert pulse, mixed with gram flour and spices and pressed through a sieve into hot oil. Bikaner has made it since the late 19th century, and the town's dry air is said to help it stay crisp. Haldiram's, now one of India's largest snack companies, started as a small shop in Bikaner in 1937. Bikaneri bhujia got a **Geographical Indication tag in 2010**, so only bhujia made in the Bikaner area can use the name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a desert bean into a national snack and a multi-billion rupee industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: A desert bean became India's favourite crunch.

sections.title: A year of fairs
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan's calendar is crowded with fairs, called melas, that mix worship, trade and fun. The biggest are livestock fairs: Pushkar in Kartik, Nagaur in winter, Tilwara on the Luni river. Desert towns hold their own: the Desert Festival at Jaisalmer in February, the Camel Festival at Bikaner in January.

Women's festivals are central. Gangaur in spring and Teej in the monsoon are about marriage, husbands and the arrival of the rains, with swings, leheriya and ghevar. And there are the modern festivals: the Jaipur Literature Festival, founded in 2006, now one of the largest literary festivals in the world, held each January.

data.name: Jaipur Literature Festival; Bikaner Camel Festival
Marwar Festival, Jodhpur; Dussehra in Kota

spotlights.name: Pushkar camel fair
spotlights.when: Kartik month, ending at the full moon (October or November)
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of camels on sand around a small town, traders in turbans, a Ferris wheel, and pilgrims bathing in the lake.
spotlights.story_md: For about two weeks in the month of Kartik, herders bring camels, horses and cattle to Pushkar to trade, while pilgrims come for the holy dip on Kartik Purnima. The fair draws an estimated 2 lakh people, many more counting the whole season. There are camel races, a longest-moustache contest, a bride contest and a tug of war between locals and foreigners. But the camel market is shrinking as camels lose value: herders report thousands fewer animals than a few decades ago. For many visitors the fair is now more photo opportunity than market.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest camel fair in the world and a barometer of the desert economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A moustache contest at a camel market at a holy lake.

spotlights.name: Gangaur
spotlights.when: Chaitra (March or April), about 18 days after Holi
spotlights.spot_it: Women in bright saris and leheriya carrying brass pots and clay images of Gauri on their heads in procession.
spotlights.story_md: Gangaur honours Gauri, or Parvati, and her marriage to Shiva. For about 18 days after Holi, married women pray for their husbands and unmarried girls pray for good ones. They make clay images of Gauri and Isar, dress them, sing to them, and on the last day carry them in procession to a lake or well for immersion. In Jaipur a royal procession with the palace's Gauri idol leaves from the City Palace; in Udaipur it ends with boats on Lake Pichola. A saying holds that Gangaur takes the festivals away with it, because no big festival follows until Teej in the monsoon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Rajasthan's most important women's festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess carried to the water so a husband stays alive.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is still mostly rural: three in four people live in villages, and a large share of them farm or herd on rain-fed land. Joint families, caste councils and community rules carry a lot of weight. Hospitality is a matter of honour, captured in the welcome *Padharo mhare des*.

The numbers show a society changing quickly from a low base. Female literacy was 52% in 2011, among the lowest in India, but the gap with men is closing among young people. Child marriage has fallen, though it remains around the national average. The state also sends huge numbers of people outward: Marwari traders over three centuries, and today migrant workers to Gujarat, Mumbai and the Gulf.

spotlights.name: The turban (pagri or safa)
spotlights.when: Everyday dress for many rural men
spotlights.spot_it: Long lengths of bright cloth wrapped high on men's heads in shapes that differ from town to town: tight, round, pointed, with a tail.
spotlights.story_md: In Rajasthan the turban is a message. Its colour, tie and length can tell you a man's region, community and sometimes the occasion. A safa is a shorter, broad wrap; a pagri is a longer, thinner cloth wound many times. Saffron, kesariya, was the colour of war and courage; white or khaki is worn for mourning; leheriya stripes and pink are for the monsoon and celebrations. Exchanging turbans was a pledge of brotherhood, and to knock off a man's turban was to insult him and his family. Many younger men no longer wear one daily, but at weddings even city grooms wear a safa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most visible piece of Rajasthani identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: A head wrapped in a message.

spotlights.name: The Bishnois and the blackbuck
spotlights.spot_it: Men in all white and women in red and maroon, near chinkara and blackbuck grazing calmly around a village.
spotlights.story_md: The Bishnoi faith was founded in 1485 by Guru Jambheshwar after a drought. Its name is said to come from bis-noi, twenty-nine, the number of its rules. They include not cutting green trees, not killing animals, and filtering water. Bishnoi villages are where you see blackbuck and chinkara walk among houses, and some women are known to breastfeed orphaned fawns. In 1998 the actor Salman Khan and others were accused of shooting blackbuck near Jodhpur; Bishnoi villagers chased them and testified. In 2018 a Jodhpur court sentenced him to five years in prison; he is out on bail while appeals continue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Bishnois are India's oldest organised conservationists.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-nine rules, one of them: do not cut a green tree.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan's famous people fall into a few groups: warrior kings and the women around them, saint-poets, and the merchant families who left the desert to build Indian business. Here are two from the twentieth century who show how the old elites adapted: a queen who went into electoral politics, and a trader's son who became one of the founders of modern Indian industry.

Others worth knowing: the shooter Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore, India's first individual Olympic silver medallist in 2004; the folk singer Ila Arun; the dancer Gulabo Sapera; the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, born in Sadulpur in Churu district; the engineer-scholar Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, who planned Jaipur; and Pramod Karan Sethi, the surgeon behind the Jaipur foot.

spotlights.name: Gayatri Devi
spotlights.spot_it: A slim woman in chiffon saris and pearls with short wavy hair, at polo grounds or on election stages.
spotlights.story_md: Born in London in 1919 to the royal family of Cooch Behar, she married Sawai Man Singh II of Jaipur in 1940 as his third wife. Cecil Beaton photographed her for *Vogue* and called her one of the most beautiful women in the world. She opened a girls' school in Jaipur in 1943, then went into politics against Indira Gandhi. In 1962 she won the Jaipur Lok Sabha seat with **192,909 of 246,516 votes**, one of the biggest margins ever recorded. During the Emergency she spent about five and a half months in Tihar jail. She died in Jaipur in 2009.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the bridge between Rajasthan's royalty and its democracy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Vogue beauty who did time in Tihar.

spotlights.name: G. D. Birla and Pilani
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man in a white Gandhi cap and dhoti beside Gandhi; or a clock tower and domed main building of a desert campus.
spotlights.story_md: Ghanshyam Das Birla was born in Pilani, a Shekhawati town, in 1894, into a Marwari trading family. He moved to Calcutta, broke into the jute business that the British dominated, and built one of India's largest industrial groups. He was also Gandhi's closest business supporter and paid many of his bills; Gandhi was shot at Birla House in Delhi in 1948. The family built schools in their home town, which became the **Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS) Pilani**, a top engineering university, in 1964. The Marwari network he belonged to also produced the Bajaj, Goenka, Singhania and Mittal families.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows how a small desert town fed India's corporate class.
spotlights.memory_hook: From a Shekhawati village to paying Gandhi's bills.

sections.title: How the desert earns
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is one of India's larger state economies, though income per person is below the national average. It earns from four things.

First, land and animals: Rajasthan is a leading grower of mustard, bajra and other oilseeds and pulses, and India's biggest producer of wool. Second, rocks: marble, sandstone, limestone for cement, zinc, lead, and in Barmer, oil. Third, sun and wind: it has more solar capacity than any other state and plans much more. Fourth, tourism: forts, palaces, deserts and weddings.

Kota is a special case: a whole city economy built on coaching for engineering and medical entrance exams, with lakhs of students a year, and a hard debate about the pressure it puts on them.

spotlights.name: Bhadla Solar Park
spotlights.spot_it: Endless rows of blue-black panels on yellow sand to the horizon, under hazy desert light.
spotlights.story_md: Bhadla, in the Thar near Phalodi, was dismissed as wasteland: hot, dusty, almost no rain. Today it holds about **2,245 MW** of solar panels across 56 square km, once listed as the largest solar park in the world. Rajasthan as a whole had more than 29 GW of solar by 2025, the most of any state, and aims for 90 GW by 2029-30. The Thar's sun is a bonanza. It is also a fight: solar parks are fenced over orans, the sacred groves and grazing land that villagers say were never wasteland, and power lines to carry the electricity cross the last habitat of the great Indian bustard.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rajasthan is becoming India's power plant, and the desert is paying a price.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wasteland that became the world's biggest sun farm.

spotlights.name: Makrana marble
spotlights.spot_it: Deep, step-sided pits of brilliant white stone, men and cranes at the bottom, cut blocks stacked on the rim.
spotlights.story_md: The white marble of the **Taj Mahal** came from Makrana, about 100 km north-west of Jaipur. So did stone for Kolkata's Victoria Memorial. Makrana marble is nearly pure calcite, which helps it keep its whiteness and take a deep polish. The quarries are now very deep pits, and work in them is dangerous: dust, heat and collapses. Rajasthan is also India's main source of other building stone, including the pink and red sandstone of Jaipur and Delhi, Kota stone floors and Jaisalmer's yellow limestone. Look at an old Indian floor and there is a good chance it came from here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rajasthan literally built much of India's architecture.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Taj Mahal is made of Rajasthan.

spotlights.name: Zawar and the zinc mines

where.label: Zawar, Udaipur district; Rampura Agucha, Bhilwara

spotlights.when: Mining from at least the first millennium BCE; smelting stopped 1812
spotlights.spot_it: Hills near Udaipur scattered with heaps of small clay tubes, the retorts used by ancient zinc smelters.
spotlights.story_md: Zinc is hard to smelt because it turns to vapour at a lower temperature than it takes to free it from ore, so the metal escapes as gas. Smelters at Zawar, 35 km from Udaipur, solved this by distillation, using thousands of small clay retorts set upside down so the vapour condensed and dripped into a cool chamber below. Mining here goes back to at least the first millennium BCE, and Zawar is described as the first place in the world to make zinc on an industrial scale; it stopped in 1812. Europe learned distillation only in the 18th century. Today Rajasthan produces nearly all of India's zinc and lead, much of it at Hindustan Zinc's Rampura Agucha mine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rajasthan had world-leading metallurgy, and still supplies the metal that stops India's steel rusting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ancient smelters made metal rain from a cloud of vapour.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
In 2025 and 2026 Rajasthan's news ran along three lines: land, safety and sport.

Land first. The Aravalli definition case and the orans march are both about who gets to decide what counts as a hill, a forest or wasteland, as solar parks and mines spread. The great Indian bustard breeding programme had its best year, with eight chicks in spring 2025. In March 2026 researchers reported that Thar dust storms carry living bacteria all the way to the Himalayas.

Safety second. A school roof collapse at Piplodi in Jhalawar killed seven children on 25 July 2025; a bus fire near Jaisalmer killed 20 on 14 October 2025; road crashes in Jodhpur and Jaipur that November killed 34; and on 17 October 2026 a minibus crash in Kota district killed eight.

And sport: the Rajasthan Royals, IPL's first champions in 2008, traded their captain Sanju Samson to Chennai for Ravindra Jadeja and Sam Curran, and under Riyan Parag reached the 2026 playoffs, losing the second qualifier.

spotlights.name: The Aravalli definition case
spotlights.spot_it: Quarried hillsides in the Aravallis: grey rock faces, trucks, and green ridges left standing beside them.
spotlights.story_md: On **20 November 2025** the Supreme Court accepted a government committee's definition of the Aravalli hills as landforms more than 100 m above the surrounding ground, a step meant to settle mining disputes. Critics said it would leave most of the range unprotected; a widely shared claim was that only 1,048 of Rajasthan's 12,081 mapped hills would qualify, a figure the court itself questioned. After protests, on **29 December 2025** a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant put the definition on hold until an independent expert opinion is available. The older Forest Survey of India definition applies meanwhile.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It decides whether mining can expand across the state's main green ridge.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mountain range that needed a court to say what counts as a mountain.

spotlights.name: The 700 km march for the orans
spotlights.spot_it: A long line of villagers in white and saffron turbans walking along a desert road with banners, a temple behind them.
spotlights.story_md: Orans are sacred groves, dedicated to local gods and heroes, where nobody cuts a tree. In Jaisalmer many were recorded in revenue maps as wasteland, which made them easy to allot for solar parks: about 44,247 hectares were allotted for 23 GW between 2023 and 2025. On **21 January 2026** about 100 villagers led by Sumer Singh Bhati set out from the Tanot Mata temple near the Pakistan border to walk about 700 km to Jaipur under a Save Oran banner, with thousands joining on the way. In December 2025 a state committee had proposed classing 2,977 hectares in three villages as oran; campaigners say that is a small start.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the 2026 version of Khejarli: villagers against a powerful project, for trees and grazing land.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sacred groves on paper called wasteland.

sections.title: Myths and what is true
sections.intro_md: Rajasthan is one of the most mythologised places in India, partly because its own bards, then British writers like James Tod, then Bollywood, all loved a good legend. Some of the most repeated stories are true, some are half true, and some are pure romance. The rule of thumb: the closer a story is to a battle or a queen, the later it was probably written down.

data.claim: Rani Padmini's beauty made Alauddin Khalji attack Chittor in 1303
data.why: The story first appears in Jayasi's poem Padmavat of 1540, 237 years later. Khalji's own chroniclers do not mention her.

data.claim: Maharana Pratap won the Battle of Haldighati
data.why: The Mughals held the field; Pratap withdrew wounded. He did win back most of Mewar in later years.

data.claim: Chetak leapt onto Man Singh's elephant
data.why: Popular painting and poetry; historians like Jadunath Sarkar call it exaggerated.

data.claim: Jodhpur is blue to keep away termites
data.why: Common explanations are caste (Brahmin houses), cooling and termites; none is established.
The Aravallis, Mount Abu, Ranthambore's forests and the Chambal valley are green; the Thar is the west.

data.claim: Rajputs and Mughals were permanent enemies
data.why: Amber, Jodhpur, Bikaner and others were Mughal allies and in-laws; Man Singh led Akbar's army at Haldighati.

data.claim: Bhangarh is the most haunted place in India
data.why: The ASI bars entry after dark, as at many monuments; the ghost stories have no evidence.

data.claim: Hawa Mahal's famous face is its front
data.why: The street facade is the back; the entrance is from the palace side.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Rajasthan is India's largest state, split by the Aravalli ridge into the Thar desert in the west and greener hills and plains in the east. Its story runs from Kalibangan's ploughed field of about 2800 BCE through Rajput kingdoms that sometimes fought and more often allied with the Mughals, to 22 units merged in seven stages between 1948 and 1956.

Remember the buildings by their numbers: Mehrangarh's 36 m walls, Jaisalmer's 99 bastions and 4,000 residents, Kumbhalgarh's 36 km wall, Hawa Mahal's 953 windows, Chand Baori's 3,500 steps, Ranakpur's 1,444 pillars. Remember the people: Amrita Devi and the 363 Bishnois, Mirabai, Pratap, Jai Singh, Gayatri Devi, G. D. Birla.

And remember the question that runs from 1730 to 2026: who gets to decide what the desert is for.

side_dish.title: The Jaipur foot: a leg designed for squatting
side_dish.body_md:
In 1968 an orthopaedic surgeon at Jaipur's SMS Medical College, Pramod Karan Sethi, and a craftsman with no medical training, Ram Chandra Sharma, set out to fix a problem Western prosthetics ignored. Artificial feet made in Europe and America assumed shoes, chairs and paved floors. Sethi's patients went barefoot, sat cross-legged, squatted to eat and cook, and walked in muddy fields.

Sharma's answer was built from what was in the bazaar: a rubber core, a wooden block and a vulcanised rubber skin that looks like a real foot and bends at the ankle. It can go barefoot, get wet and squat. It was cheap enough to give away: a charity, Bhagwan Mahaveer Viklang Sahayata Samiti, founded in 1975, fits it free, often in a single day.

The foot has been fitted to landmine survivors in Afghanistan, Cambodia and many other countries. The dancer Sudha Chandran, who lost a leg in 1981, danced again on one, and her story became the films *Mayuri* and *Naache Mayuri*. Sethi received the Ramon Magsaysay Award and the Padma Shri in 1981. In 2009 a low-cost Jaipur Knee developed with Stanford students was named one of *Time*'s best inventions.

The design lesson: the best product starts from how people actually live. The Jaipur foot was never patented, so it spread, and quality varies for the same reason.

offline_task.title: Ten words of Rajasthani
offline_task.body_md:
Learn these ten and try them on someone from Rajasthan, or say them out loud while you look at today's pictures.

1. **Khamma ghani**: the standard respectful greeting, roughly 'much forgiveness'.
2. **Padharo mhare des**: welcome to my land; also the most famous folk song.
3. **Hukum**: sir, or yes sir; a word of respect used everywhere in Mewar and Marwar.
4. **Thane**: you (respectful).
5. **Mhane**: me.
6. **Kaain**: what.
7. **Ghano**: very, a lot.
8. **Choro / chhori**: boy / girl.
9. **Baisa**: respectful word for a woman, especially of a Rajput family.
10. **Ram Ram sa**: hello, used across communities.

Then listen to any recording of *Kesariya balam padharo mhare des* and see how many words you can catch.

best_facts.fact: In 1730, 363 Bishnois were killed one by one as they hugged khejri trees to stop the Maharaja of Marwar's men cutting them.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tree-hugging protest, 250 years before Chipko, paid for in lives.

best_facts.fact: About 20,000 rats live in the Karni Mata temple at Deshnoke. If you kill one by accident, custom says you replace it with a rat made of gold or silver.
best_facts.why_surprising: A temple where rats are relatives.

best_facts.fact: Jaipur's sundial, the Samrat Yantra, is 27 m tall and tells local time to about two seconds; its shadow moves about 1 mm every second.
best_facts.why_surprising: Stone, not electronics, and it still works.

best_facts.fact: Hawa Mahal's famous street face, with 953 windows, is the back of the building.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most photographed facade in India is a rear wall.

best_facts.fact: At Haldighati in 1576, Akbar's army was commanded by a Rajput, Man Singh of Amber, and Maharana Pratap's front line by an Afghan, Hakim Khan Sur.
best_facts.why_surprising: The famous Rajput-versus-Mughal battle had Rajputs and Muslims on both sides.

best_facts.fact: Jaipur blue pottery contains no clay. It is made from quartz powder, glass, fuller's earth, borax and gum.
Kalibangan in Rajasthan has a ploughed field from about 2800 BCE, among the oldest ever excavated, and evidence of an earthquake about 2600 BCE.
best_facts.why_surprising: Farmers ploughed here almost 5,000 years ago.

best_facts.fact: Jaipur was painted pink in 1876 for one visitor, the Prince of Wales, and has stayed pink since.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city's identity came from a single welcome.

best_facts.fact: The Thar is the most densely populated desert in the world, with about 83 people per square km.
best_facts.why_surprising: Deserts are supposed to be empty.

best_facts.fact: Great Indian bustard numbers fell from about 1,260 in 1969 to fewer than 150 in 2018. The main killer is power lines.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the heaviest flying birds is dying from wires.

best_facts.fact: About 4,000 people still live inside Jaisalmer Fort, built in 1156, and their plumbing is helping to undermine its walls.

best_facts.why_surprising: Hindu family history kept by Muslim musicians.

best_facts.why_surprising: A killing ground became a refuge.

best_facts.fact: Zawar near Udaipur made zinc by distillation on an industrial scale long before Europe learned how.
best_facts.why_surprising: Medieval Rajasthan led the world in a hard metallurgy.

best_facts.fact: The white marble of the Taj Mahal was quarried at Makrana in Rajasthan.
best_facts.why_surprising: Agra's monument is built of Rajasthan.
